title: The application the viewer watches freeze is not the one the reviewer opens
evidence: Scene 3's modal is titled 'OES Supply Base 2026-A — your application', status 'Qualified', 'Submitted Mar 12, 2026', commitments 'RUTF 34,000 cartons/month · NG, SD · 28 day lead time', and its footer reads 'The reviewer's decision WAS MADE against the left-hand column' — past tense, a round that closed months ago. Scene 4's modal is 'Review — Savanna Nutrients Ltd', 'Frozen Jul 19, 2026', commitments 'RUTF 39,000 cartons/month · NG, SD · 14 day lead time', drawn from the 2026-B review queue. The same supplier, two different submissions to two different rounds, presented as one continuous story. Scene 3's own page also shows both rows in 'Your applications' (2026-B Submitted, 2026-A Qualified), so the correct one was on screen and the recipe deliberately clicked the older one (its note: 'open the application the qualification came from').
why_it_matters: The whole point of scene 3 is that the frozen column is what Tomas is about to judge. If the frozen column belongs to a round already decided, the setup does not set up the payoff, and the narration's 'the decision Tomas is about to make stays reconstructable a year from now' has no on-screen referent. This is invisible to any per-scene judge — each frame is internally consistent.
options: Point scene 3 at the 2026-B row (still 'Submitted') so the frozen profile is literally the one scene 4 opens; the 'changed since' certification badge is the reason the scene exists and can be seeded on that submission instead.
Keep the 2026-A application but re-cut the narration to say a past decision is still reconstructable, and move the 'about to be judged' language into scene 4 where the pending submission actually is.
Seed one submission only — remove the duplicate 2026-A/2026-B pair for Savanna — so there is nothing for the camera to pick wrongly.

title: The qualification decision is never committed, and the registry contradicts what the decision promised
evidence: Scene 4 selects Qualify on RUTF and Reject on Therapeutic milk; the panel reads 'RUTF — qualified until Jan 20, 2028' and the 'Record decision' button sits unclicked at the bottom of the frame — the recipe's last action for the scene is a 3.2s hold after the Reject click. Scene 5 then shows the registry filtered to RUTF + Nigeria: three rows (Kano Therapeutic Foods Feb 17 2027, Lagos NutriWorks Feb 19 2027, Savanna Nutrients Feb 18 2027). Savanna's EARLIEST EXPIRY is Feb 18, 2027 — not the Jan 20, 2028 scene 4 just promised — and it sits in an ordinary alphabetical row indistinguishable from two suppliers who were already there.
why_it_matters: Scenes 4 and 5 are the causal hinge of act one: a decision creates a registry entry, and the registry is nothing but the set of live qualifications. As shot, the decision is abandoned mid-gesture and the registry shows a pre-existing state, so the viewer is told the mechanism rather than shown it. Exactly the same class of defect the run just fixed at the other end (award → contract), still open here.
options: Click 'Record decision' on camera and let scene 5 open unfiltered so Savanna's row appears (or its expiry changes) as a visible consequence — the same 'the award produced this contract' move that repaired scene 9.
If the decision must stay uncommitted, cut the promised date from the panel or make scene 5 show the qualification that scene 4's date actually produces, so the two frames stop disagreeing.
Add a one-beat reaction shot between 4 and 5 — the toast or the registry count moving 2 → 3 — rather than a scene transition that hides the state change.

title: Scene 7 is contained entirely inside scene 8's frame
evidence: Scene 7 and scene 8 are the same modal, 'RUTF Northeast Nigeria Q3 2026', at adjacent scroll offsets. Every row scene 7 shows is present in scene 8 with identical values and identical order: Maiduguri — Savanna 42.29 / tech 91, Kano 43.77 / 60, Lagos 45.79 / 83, Faso 48.64 / 82; Djibo — Faso 41.85 / 88, Savanna 45.90 / 79, Kano 46.42 / 61, Lagos 47.31 / 74. Scene 8 adds only the two 'Awarded —' badges and a toast. Scene 7's narrated point (the leader on Maiduguri is not the leader on Djibo) is fully legible in scene 8's own frame.
why_it_matters: Two of nine beats are spent on one surface, and the earlier of the two is strictly a subset of the later. Cutting scene 7 would cost the story almost nothing, which by the rubric caps escalation at 3 — and it is the beat immediately before the run's biggest moment, so it drains momentum where it is least affordable.
options: Cut scene 7 and open scene 8 on the un-awarded comparison, sorting or highlighting per lot before awarding — one beat that both reveals the split leaders and acts on them.

Keep both but make scene 7 do something the frame cannot already say: sort by technical score so the price/quality tension is on camera, or bring in the third lot (Damaturu, 35,000) that neither scene currently reads.
Reassign the recovered time to the close, which is the more under-served end (see arc-close-lands-on-an-empty-schedule).

title: The finale now resolves the right contract, but its bottom half is an empty state and it calls itself the midpoint
evidence: Scene 9 opens OES-C-2026-NG2 — 'Savanna Nutrients Ltd · Maiduguri, Nigeria', '60,000 cartons RUTF delivered to Maiduguri · awarded under RUTF Northeast Nigeria Q3 2026, Jul 28, 2026' — which is the lot awarded on camera one scene earlier. The upper card is the run's densest new material (US Government, FY2026 Emergency Food Security — Horn of Africa & Sahel, IATI US-GOV-1-OES-OES-C-2026-NG2, OBLIGATED USD 2,537,400, UNIT PRICE 42.29). The lower half is 'No consignments raised against this contract yet', 'DISBURSED USD 0.00', '0 confirmed at destination · 60,000 outstanding' — under narration claiming 'what carries it out is a contract, carrying the delivery schedule into execution' and 'the same record is what the supply chain moves against'. The narration also says 'This is the midpoint'. Separately, the opening's stated question — 'who is qualified to supply RUTF to north-east Nigeria today' — is answered in scene 5, not at the close.
why_it_matters: The chain is now correct, which is the real win over the previous run, but a finale whose largest element is an empty state and whose narration announces it is not the end reads as stopping rather than landing. The viewer's last impression is a blank delivery table.
options: Seed one or two consignments against OES-C-2026-NG2 so the delivery schedule has rows and DISBURSED is non-zero — the claim 'trace a dollar to a carton' then has a picture.
Scroll the close to the funding card and end there, cutting the empty schedule out of frame, and re-cut the narration to promise the money trail rather than the movement.

Add a short callback line that closes the opening's loop explicitly — the folder of PDFs became a registry, a tender, and a funded contract — so the close answers the question the opening asked instead of introducing a new act.

title: Nine frames in one shell, and the app's most distinct surface appears only as backdrop
evidence: Every frame is the same chrome: left nav, green accent, header pill. Shapes break down as one dashboard (1), three full-page tables (2, 5, 6) and five modals (3, 4, 7, 8, 9), with 7 and 8 the same modal at adjacent scroll offsets. After scene 1's small bar chart there is no chart, no map and no form in the run. Meanwhile the Command centre — 'Pipeline by corridor', with IPC severity chips (Séno IPC 2, Yagha IPC 4), 0% coverage chips and a gap column — is visible behind scene 9's modal and is never shown as a frame of its own. Routed CONCEPT, not PRODUCT: the surface exists and the narrative simply passes through it to open a modal.
why_it_matters: By the middle of the run the eye has habituated — scenes 5, 6, 7 and 8 are four consecutive frames of rows of text in the same container. One genuinely different shape in that stretch would reset attention, and the product already has one sitting unused.
options: Hold on the Command centre for a beat before opening the contract in scene 9 — corridor pipeline and IPC severity is the only frame in the run that looks like a crisis rather than a spreadsheet, and it motivates why the tender exists.
Give scene 5 the registry coverage visual (the bar chart from scene 1's 'Registry coverage by category') or the count moving under the filters, so it is not a third static table.

Shoot scene 6 from Amina's seat — the supplier's Solicitations tab — which changes the chrome, changes the persona badge, and is the only framing that could actually show the eligibility rule the scene claims.
